newsitem.title: USA: Senate will not seek to amend forex law this year.
newsitem.headline: Senate will not seek to amend forex law this year.

text.p: A Senate bill to overhaul U.S. commodity futures regulation will be introduced next week, but the proposal will not seek to address a problematic section of current law governing foreign exchange trading, a spokesman for the Senate Agriculture Committee said.

Committee chairman Sen. Dick Lugar and Sen. Pat Leahy will introduce a bill next week to amend the Commodity Exchange Act, the spokesman said. But a section of the bill on the 1974 "Treasury Amendment" will be set aside until next year.

Under the 1974 law, interbank forex trading is exempt from the jusrisdiction of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. But ambiguities have arisen concerning the scope of the amendment, and the Supreme Court will decide a case on the issue next term.

CFTC and Treasury Department officials have been working for months to craft a compromise solution that would not endanger the forex market. Lugar and Leahy had hoped the agencies would find a solution by September, but the agencies recently told the committee they would need at least until the end of the year, the committee spokesman said.

The Lugar-Leahy proposal is expected to include several changes requested by U.S. futures exchanges, including allowing the exchanges to begin trading in new contracts far more quickly than under current rules.

In light of the Sumitomo Corp copper trading scandal, the bill is also expected to expand the jurisdiction of the CFTC over foreign boards of trade that accept delivery in the United States. Sumitomo conducted most of its copper trading on the London Metal Exchange but stashed copper in an LME warehouse in California.
Wall Street has been pushing the Senate to stay out of the Treasury Amendment dispute.
In a letter to Lugar and Leahy sent on Thursday, the Public Securities Association warned that changing the amendment could wreak havoc on the markets.

"We urge you in the strongest possible terms to refrain from redrafting the so-called Treasury Amendment," PSA executive vice president Micah Green wrote in the letter. "Any regulatory redundancy or overlap caused by your legislation could jeopardize the market's vital efficiency and liquidity."
CFTC officials have generally opposed the Lugar-Leahy reform package.

Commissioner John Tull said this summer, while he was acting chairman of the commission, that it was too soon to reform the current rules since the CFTC was still investigating the Sumitomo scandal. But Tull said the CFTC would abide by Congress's wishes.
New chairwoman Brooksley Born holds similiar views, one CFTC official said.
